name: Sound + motion relationship
controls: What role audio plays and how picture and sound are locked together: whether music, voice or effects lead, which sound families accent the motion, and how audio anticipates, reinforces and bridges visual events.
question: What should the video sound like, and how tightly should motion follow the audio?
notes: Pick the lead (silent, music-led, voiceover-led or SFX-led) plus up to two sound-design families; the sync facet sets how tightly picture follows audio. Much product motion is watched muted (social autoplay, web heroes), so any piece that isn't silent-by-design should still read with sound off. Terminology is loose: 'sound design' can mean the whole audio layer or only the effects; 'swoosh' and 'whoosh' are the same thing; 'sonic logo', 'sonic branding' and 'audio logo' overlap. Sound effects that sit on a musical grid should follow the track's key and tempo, or they fight the music. Human perception tolerates audio arriving slightly after picture far better than before it: keep sync within about +/- 1-2 frames, and if in doubt let sound trail by a frame rather than lead. Mix hierarchy: voiceover > key SFX > music; duck music 6-10 dB under VO.

options.what: Cuts, key poses and hits placed on the music's beats and bar lines.
options.prompt: Detect the track's BPM and downbeats; put every scene change on a downbeat or bar line and every key pose or impact on a beat. Secondary motion on half or quarter beats. Keep entrances <= 1 beat long so they land on the grid.

options.what: On-screen words and visual changes timed to the exact moment each word is spoken.
options.prompt: Use a word-level transcript with timestamps; make each keyword appear within +/- 2 frames of its spoken onset and change scenes 100-200 ms after sentence ends. Emphasize stressed words with scale or weight at the moment they're said.

options.what: Every visual impact (landing, slam, collision, click) gets a matched sound on the same frame.
options.prompt: Pair each visual impact with a sound on the exact frame of contact: logo lands -> low impact; button press -> click; card slams -> thud. Match sound weight to visual scale; do not add sound to non-impact moves.

options.what: Sound starts before the visual event (riser, reverse swell, inhale) so the viewer expects it.
options.prompt: Start a riser or reverse swell 0.5-2 s before each major reveal so its peak lands on the reveal frame. Optionally drop to silence for 200-500 ms just before the hit to heighten it.

options.what: Sound carries the viewer across a visual transition: a whoosh over a wipe, or audio from the next scene starting early (J-cut) or lingering (L-cut).
options.prompt: Cover every visual transition with sound: whooshes centered on the midpoint of wipes and camera moves, and J-cuts where the next scene's audio begins 8-15 frames before its picture. Never let a transition happen in dead silence unless silence is the intent.

options.what: Designed to be watched without audio; all meaning is carried visually.
options.looks: Burned-in captions or headline cards, clear visual cause and effect, text legible at feed size.
options.motion: Motion carries rhythm and emphasis that sound would normally supply: stronger visual accents, holds, and scale changes.
options.use: Landing-page heroes, social autoplay, in-product animations, digital signage.
options.vs: Muted-autoplay-safe pieces can still have sound; silent motion is designed with no audio track at all.
options.prompt: Design with no audio track. Carry emphasis visually: add 1-2 frame scale pops or flashes where a sound hit would be, put all dialogue-equivalent information in on-screen text, and give text >= 1 s per 3 words. The piece must be fully understood muted.

options.what: A music track is the primary audio and sets structure, pacing and emotion.
options.looks: Visual structure mirrors the track: intro, build, drop, outro.
options.motion: Cuts and hits locked to the beat; intensity follows the arrangement.
options.use: Launch films, trailers, recaps, brand films, social.
options.conveys: Emotion and energy set by the music.
options.vs: Beat-driven pacing is a visual rhythm; music-led means an actual track leads. Music under a voiceover is voiceover-led, not music-led.
options.prompt: Choose the track first and map its sections with timestamps. Structure scenes to its phrases (4- or 8-bar blocks), put the hero reveal on the drop or biggest accent, and fade or cut the music on a bar line at the end (never mid-phrase).

options.what: Narration carries the message; visuals illustrate and reinforce it.
options.looks: Visuals that match each line; on-screen keywords echoing the VO; captions.
options.motion: Scene changes on sentence boundaries, emphasis on stressed words, holds in pauses.
options.vs: Music-led puts emotion first; VO-led puts information first. A talking-head video shows the speaker; VO is off-screen.
options.prompt: Write and record (or synthesize) the VO first; time visuals to it. Change scenes at sentence ends, echo 1-3 keywords per sentence on screen as they're spoken, duck music 6-10 dB under the voice, and leave 0.3-0.6 s of breathing space between sentences.

options.what: Designed sound effects drive the audio experience, with little or no music.
options.looks: Visual events with strong physicality: clicks, snaps, impacts, material interactions.
options.motion: Every significant motion has a matched sound; motion is timed to make sounds land cleanly.
options.use: Product films (hardware, UI), ASMR-style content, logo stings, teasers.
options.conveys: Tactility and precision; the product feels physical.
options.vs: UI sound is one SFX family; SFX-led means effects are the lead layer overall.
options.prompt: Make effects the lead audio layer; music absent or a quiet bed. Give every meaningful motion a designed sound (clicks, slides, impacts, material textures) on its exact frame; leave silence between events so each sound reads. Keep effects in one sonic palette (e.g. all soft, dry, close-miked).

options.what: Short, clean sounds for interface events: taps, toggles, notifications, success, error.
options.looks: UI interactions shown on screen: clicks, toggles, messages arriving.
options.motion: Micro-interactions with crisp timing; sound fires at the moment of state change.
options.use: Product demos, UI showcases, app promos.
options.vs: Clicks are one UI sound; UI sound is the whole family. 'Earcon' is the HCI term for abstract interface sounds.
options.prompt: Add short (30-200 ms), soft, pitched interface sounds at each state change: tap on press, subtle tick on toggle, rising two-note chime on success, low muted tone on error. Keep them quiet (-18 to -24 dB below VO) and consistent in timbre.

options.what: Recorded or recreated everyday sounds (paper, fabric, footsteps, objects) synced to on-screen action.
options.looks: Tangible objects and materials on screen; hands, papers, devices.
options.motion: Physical, weighted motion that implies contact and texture.
options.use: Hardware films, illustrated explainers wanting warmth, stop-motion, craft brands.
options.vs: Designed SFX (whooshes, synth hits) are abstract; foley is real-world texture. The term comes from film post-production (after Jack Foley).
options.prompt: Add real-world sounds matched to materials: paper slides and folds for cards, fabric rustle for soft shapes, glass or metal taps for hardware, placed on contact frames. Keep them close and dry; avoid synthetic whooshes so the world feels physical.

options.what: Air-movement sounds that accompany fast moves, wipes and camera sweeps.
options.looks: Fast lateral moves, wipes, zooms, spins.
options.motion: Fast transitions with motion blur; the whoosh peaks at maximum velocity.
options.use: Transitions in launch films, trailers, social, broadcast.
options.vs: Risers build over seconds; whooshes last 0.2-1 s and follow movement. Overuse is a common amateur tell.
options.prompt: Place a whoosh on fast moves only (transitions, camera sweeps), 0.3-0.8 s long, with its loudest point aligned to the motion's peak velocity (usually the midpoint). Pan with the direction of travel. No more than one whoosh per 2 s.

options.what: Tiny, sharp transient sounds for precise events: button presses, snapping into place, counters.
options.looks: Buttons, cursors, toggles, grid snaps, ticking numbers.
options.motion: Precise, snappy moves that end in firm settles.
options.use: UI demos, data count-ups, typographic pieces, technical films.
options.vs: Pops are rounder and playful; clicks are dry and exact.
options.prompt: Add dry, short clicks (<= 50 ms) on precise events: cursor presses, elements snapping to grid, digits ticking during count-ups (thin them to every 2nd-3rd digit if the count is fast). Keep levels low and consistent.

options.what: Round, bright, playful transients for elements appearing, bubbles and scale-ins.
options.looks: Icons, stickers, chat bubbles and shapes scaling in.
options.motion: Scale-in with overshoot, springy arrivals, staggered pop-ins.
options.use: Playful explainers, social content, consumer apps, chat UI.
options.vs: Clicks are precise and dry; pops are round and cheerful. Pitch-shifted pops for staggered sequences are a common trope.
options.prompt: Add short round pops on scale-in arrivals, timed to the overshoot peak. For staggered sequences, step the pitch upward by a semitone per element (max 5-6 steps) and keep each pop under 120 ms.

options.what: Heavy, low-frequency hits that give weight to landings, slams and reveals.
options.looks: Big type slamming in, logo landings, cuts to black, hero reveals.
options.motion: Fast arrivals with abrupt stops, camera shake, flash frames.
options.use: Trailers, launch films, sports, logo stings.
options.vs: Clicks are tiny; impacts are cinematic. 'Stinger' also means a short musical sting or a broadcast transition; usage varies.
options.prompt: Place a low, heavy impact (sub-bass thump + transient) on the exact frame of the biggest landings only, max 3-5 per minute. Pair with a 2-4 frame visual shake or flash; follow with 0.5-1 s of decay or silence.

options.what: Sounds that rise in pitch, volume or density over several seconds to build tension toward a moment.
options.looks: Accelerating visuals, tightening framing, countdowns, pre-reveal builds.
options.motion: Acceleration and escalation that peak on the riser's end.
options.vs: Whooshes follow a single movement; risers build over 2-8 s. Reverse cymbals and reverse reverbs are short risers.
options.prompt: Start a riser 2-6 s before a reveal and synchronize visual escalation (faster cuts, zoom creep, increasing brightness) to it. End the riser either directly into an impact on the reveal frame or into 200-500 ms of silence before the hit.

options.what: The moment music or sound releases after a build, usually a heavy beat entry or a sudden fall-away.
options.looks: The hero reveal, the product name, a scene explosion into color.
options.motion: Maximum visual release on the drop frame: scale, color flood, burst of elements.
options.use: Trailers, social ads, event openers, music visualizers.
options.vs: A riser is the build; the drop is the release. 'Downlifter' is the falling sound effect, not a musical drop.
options.prompt: Align the single biggest visual moment (reveal, color flood, burst) to the drop's first downbeat within +/- 1 frame. Hold visual stillness or darkness for 0.3-0.5 s immediately before it, then release.

options.what: Electronic, synthesized tones, sweeps and glitches that give motion a digital character.
options.looks: Tech and AI visuals, HUDs, data, particles, glitch.
options.motion: Data flows, scans, glitch frames, glowing activations.
options.use: AI products, developer tools, futuristic brands, gaming.
options.vs: UI sound is functional and subtle; synth effects are expressive and atmospheric. Foley is organic; synth is electronic.
options.prompt: Use synthesized tones for digital events: filtered sweeps on scans (matching scan duration), short blips on data points, bit-crushed glitches on glitch frames, tonal pads on glowing activations. Tune them to the music's key.

options.what: A continuous background bed (room tone, nature, drone, texture) that sets place and mood without rhythm.
options.looks: Atmospheric, slow visuals; environments; abstract loops.
options.motion: Slow, continuous motion without hard hits.
options.use: Brand films, installations, meditative pieces, teasers, backgrounds.
options.vs: Music has melody and rhythm; ambience doesn't. 'Atmos' is also short for Dolby Atmos; context decides.
options.prompt: Lay a continuous ambient bed (drone, room tone or environment) at low level for the whole piece, evolving slowly (filter or volume changes over 5-10 s). Avoid rhythmic elements; let occasional sparse SFX sit on top.

options.what: A short, ownable sound signature (1-3 s) paired with the logo.
options.looks: Logo reveal or sting at the end of the piece.
options.motion: Logo motion choreographed note for note with the sonic logo.
options.use: End of ads, app launches, device startups, broadcast idents.
options.vs: A jingle is a longer sung melody; a sonic logo is a brief signature. Logo sting is the visual counterpart.
options.prompt: Pair the logo animation with a 1-3 s sonic signature: map each note or hit to a stage of the logo motion (first note = first shape appears, final note = mark completes). End the motion exactly when the sound resolves, then hold still.
